title: Ageing with grace
hook: old age as a season, not a loss
tomorrow: Simran's college essay is stuck. who does she ask?

segments.voice: Yesterday, all creatures: every creature carries the light, down to a sparrow with a bent wing. This morning Baba Kartar is at the breakfast table.

Every feed has an ad that promises to make you look younger. Baba Kartar would not be the target audience. His hands shake now; his tea rattles on the saucer, and Simran, who notices everything, pretends not to. He doesn't pretend. He lifts the cup, watches it tremble, and says, my hands are in the fourth watch. Then he drinks. Fourth watch of what? It sounds like a riddle, and it is one. It comes from Guru Nanak, in Sri Raag, Ang 74, in a poem called the Pehre. And the strange thing is the shape of it: a whole human life, told as one single night.
screen: `AN AD TO LOOK YOUNGER.` → `MY HANDS ARE IN THE FOURTH WATCH.` → `A LIFE TOLD AS ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Why a night? Guru Nanak divides it into watches, the way a night guard's shift is divided. In the first watch, in paraphrase, the soul arrives by the Command. In the next, youth, and forgetting. Then the body, and wealth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field. And all the way through he speaks to the listener by an odd, warm name: O my merchant friend. A trader, passing through, with something to trade. Here's the thing to tell someone tonight: Guru Nanak's poem about growing old calls you his merchant friend in every watch. Now the puzzle's answer. A night isn't a day that went wrong. It has its own hours and its own work. The poem doesn't sweeten the fourth watch; the body tires, and the reaper is real. But the call in the fourth watch is the same as in the first: remember the Name. No watch is too late. None is the wrong one. Baba Kartar's reading is simple. My hands shake, he says, and they still fold. Each watch has its own work. This one is mine.
screen: `A LIFE TOLD AS ONE NIGHT.` · `O MY MERCHANT FRIEND.` · `THE FOURTH WATCH ISN'T SWEETENED.` · `EVERY WATCH: REMEMBER.` · then, large: `EVERY SEASON.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up. Starting at your feet, give each part of your body a silent thank you for one thing it did today: feet for the walk, hands for the cup, eyes for this screen. Go slowly, and thank the parts that ache too.
Ageing with grace. In Guru Nanak's Pehre, old age is the fourth watch of one night: a season with its own work, not the loss of the day.
The line to keep: every season, the fourth watch too, each with its own work. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Pehre of Sri Raag read and sung in the Guru Granth Sahib; elders in many Sikh families keep their daily prayers into old age, often reading from a gutka or listening when their eyes tire.
